title: Salt, Fire, and the Weight of Returning
verdict: Christopher Nolan turns Homer's voyage into a stern, tactile spectacle whose roughest passages still carry the shock of bodies meeting sea, stone and history.
excerpt: The gods recede, the water darkens, and Matt Damon's exhausted face becomes the film's most persuasive special effect.
content:
## A sea with weight

Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey* begins by stripping antiquity of its museum glass. Wood swells with water. Bronze looks heavy enough to bruise the hand holding it. Fire is not an orange wash added behind an actor but a poor, nervous source of light that leaves half a face unreadable. The 70mm IMAX frame does not make this world grand by polishing it. It makes distance exhausting. A ship on open water appears fragile because the water has no edge.

Matt Damon's Odysseus belongs to that material world. Damon gives him no heroic float. His shoulders tighten before his voice does; his silences have the dull drag of a man counting what his cleverness has cost. Nolan has often built films around intelligence moving faster than feeling. Here, intelligence is slower and dirtier. Each solution leaves a residue. Damon carries that residue without decorating it as nobility.

The film's gods are scarce. Zendaya's Athena appears with the clean interruption of a thought that may or may not be divine, while the monsters arrive through hide, breath, darkness and scale. Nolan's skepticism is productive up to a point. The Cyclops sequence works because the creature occupies space before it becomes an effect: the cave narrows, bodies bunch together, and every sound seems to have struck rock on its way to the ear. The supernatural is most vivid when the camera treats it as an animal fact.

## Motion without lightness

The voyage proceeds through recollection, but the fractured chronology is unusually easy to follow. Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, and Telemachus, played by Tom Holland, wait in Ithaca while Odysseus's years away surface in long blocks of memory. Nolan does not use time as a lock to be opened. He uses it as pressure. Home exists in one tempo; war and wandering exist in another. The cut between them is less a surprise than a wound repeatedly touched.

Ludwig Göransson's score drives hard, sometimes too hard. Drums and low brass can turn a physical ordeal into an announcement of ordeal. The better stretches let rope, surf and labored breathing set the pulse. A night raid illuminated by unstable fire has more force before the orchestra arrives to certify it. Nolan trusts the image, then occasionally mistrusts his own trust.

The enormous cast produces flashes rather than a uniform weave. Samantha Morton's Circe has a cold, unhurried presence; Charlize Theron's Calypso makes stillness feel narcotic; Lupita Nyong'o cuts through the martial gloom with a face that refuses submission. Some encounters pass too quickly, reduced to stations on a famous route. Scylla and Charybdis feel crossed off where Circe feels inhabited. Scale cannot supply duration.

## The face at the end of the epic

Hathaway understands that waiting is an action. Her Penelope listens with the vigilance of someone defending a house by controlling what others are allowed to know. Holland's Telemachus is more exposed, hope and embarrassment moving across him before he can arrange either into a public expression. Their scenes keep Ithaca from becoming a destination marker. Home has continued in Odysseus's absence; it has acquired its own weather.

Nolan's directness in the later movement is bracing. The machinery of chronology quiets, and the film allows recognition to depend on faces, posture and the terrible gap between memory and presence. Damon becomes smaller as Odysseus nears what he wanted. The warrior who survived by naming himself nobody must occupy his own name again.

*The Odyssey* is uneven because its appetite exceeds even its long running time. Yet its finest images do not feel like illustrations of Homer or demonstrations of IMAX. They feel discovered: a sail pulling against wind, fire sliding along a bronze edge, Hathaway holding a room still, Damon looking at home as though distance had become a substance inside him. The film returns an old story to the pressure of surfaces. Salt remains after the spectacle recedes.

title: A Good Song in a Very Expensive Echo
verdict: The live-action Moana has enough warmth, rhythm and star power to keep a family crowd happy, but it spends most of that energy proving the animated film never needed replacing.
excerpt: Catherine Laga'aia gives the remake a pulse of its own whenever the digital ocean and corporate memory stop crowding her out.
content:
## The girl is alive; the remake is on life support

Here is the strange good news about Disney's live-action *Moana*: Catherine Laga'aia is wonderful. She does not imitate the animated heroine's bounce or treat a beloved movie like an audition she is afraid to fail. She plants her feet, sings “How Far I'll Go” with a clear, open force, and makes Moana's curiosity look physical. You see the horizon tug at her. For a few minutes, the remake stops defending its existence and becomes a musical with a new young star at its center.

Then the movie remembers the assignment. The ocean rises in the same comic shapes. The pig and chicken hit their marks. A line you remember approaches, waits for recognition, and lands exactly where the old line landed. Thomas Kail directs with speed and professional brightness, but the film is trapped inside the audience's memory of another film. It cannot surprise us without risking the brand, and it cannot repeat the original without becoming a very expensive echo.

The island scenes expose the problem first. Real bodies should add friction: sand under a foot, a crowd that cannot move with animated precision, weather changing the color of a face. Sometimes they do. Rena Owen's Tala has a loose, mischievous warmth, and John Tui gives Moana's father a tired authority rather than generic obstruction. But the production keeps polishing the world until the live setting feels almost as sealed as animation, only heavier.

## Maui walks off with the movie, naturally

Dwayne Johnson was always hiding inside the animated Maui, so letting him occupy the whole body is the remake's easiest and best decision. He knows where the jokes bend, where to let vanity swell, and when a grin should confess that the demigod is scared. “You're Welcome” works because Johnson does not sing it as a sacred franchise object. He plays it as a sales pitch delivered by a man who believes his own brochure.

His scenes with Laga'aia have the rough playfulness the movie needs. She refuses to become his straight woman; he refuses to surrender the frame without a fight. Their argument has rhythm. When the digital tattoo on Maui's chest interrupts him, the effect belongs to the performance rather than sitting on top of it. That is the rare remake trick worth keeping: animation and flesh heckling each other in the same shot.

The effects elsewhere are handsome and fussy. The water gleams, the boats cut clean lines, and the Kakamora arrive like a studio note demanding that the picture wake up. But brightness is not buoyancy. The animated film could change shape in an instant; this one has to haul every fantasy object into photographic space and explain its weight. The effort shows. You can feel the computers sweating beneath the ocean.

## What exactly did the flesh add?

The songs survive because they were built to survive almost anything. Lin-Manuel Miranda and Opetaia Foa'i wrote melodies that carry character before scenery, and Kail's theater instincts keep the musical numbers moving forward. A new song adds time but not necessity. The old numbers still do the emotional lifting, which makes the remake's competence slightly embarrassing: every pleasure sends you back to the source.

I do not buy the easy claim that the film is lifeless. Laga'aia is alive. Owen is alive. Johnson, when he stops posing for the invisible poster, is very alive. Children hearing these songs in a crowded theater may have a terrific afternoon, and that counts. A family movie does not owe adults a dissertation on why it was financed.

But criticism does not owe the financing amnesia. The 2016 *Moana* remains faster, stranger and freer, and this version follows it so closely that fidelity becomes timidity. The remake succeeds whenever a performer pushes against the template and goes slack whenever the template wins. I smiled often, tapped my foot, and left wondering why a corporation spent all that money to make spontaneity work twice as hard.
